name: Oleocanthal
description: Phenolic compound in EVOO that inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes — the same targets as ibuprofen — producing anti-inflammatory effects

name: Hydroxytyrosol
description: Potent antioxidant polyphenol in EVOO; scavenges free radicals and reduces LDL oxidation

name: Oleic acid
description: Monounsaturated fatty acid (>70% of EVOO); promotes reverse cholesterol transport and reduces vascular inflammation

name: Oleuropein
description: Polyphenol precursor abundant in Cretan EVOO; anti-inflammatory and cardioprotective effects

name: Apigenin
description: Flavone abundant in Sideritis scardica; anti-inflammatory (COX inhibition) comparable to indomethacin in animal models; gastroprotective

name: Luteolin
description: Flavone in Sideritis scardica; anti-inflammatory and antioxidant; synergistic effects with apigenin

name: Verbascoside (acteoside)
description: Phenylpropanoid glycoside in Sideritis; binds NLRP3 inflammasome (Kd 0.67 μM) and NF-κB (Kd 0.01 μM); key mechanistic driver of anti-inflammatory activity

name: Hydroxy-cinnamic acids
description: Class of phenolic acids in Sideritis (includes rosmarinic acid); implicated in monoamine reuptake inhibition and cerebral blood flow increase underlying cognitive effects

name: Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA)
description: Plant-derived omega-3 fatty acid; purslane is the richest known leafy vegetable source; anti-inflammatory precursor to EPA and DHA; lowers LDL and triglycerides

name: Portulacaxanthin
description: Yellow betalain pigment unique to purslane; potent antioxidant; scavenges free radicals and reduces oxidative stress markers

name: Kaempferol
description: Flavonol polyphenol in purslane; inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α and IL-6; contributes to joint and vascular anti-inflammatory effects

name: Purslane mucilage polysaccharides
description: Gel-forming soluble fibre in purslane; acts as a prebiotic and bulk-forming agent; supports gut motility and colonic transit time reduction

name: Vitamin K2 (menaquinone)
description: Produced during fermentation of aged hard cheese; activates matrix Gla-protein which prevents calcium from depositing in artery walls; may explain cheese's paradoxical cardiovascular protection despite saturated fat content

name: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)
description: Natural trans-fatty acid found at higher concentrations in sheep and goat dairy from pasture-fed animals; anti-inflammatory and potentially antiatherogenic

name: ACE-inhibitory casein peptides
description: Bioactive peptides released from casein during cheese fermentation and digestion; inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) — the same target as antihypertensive drugs; identified in cultures of Graviera-native L. plantarum strains

name: Lactobacillus plantarum (native LAB)
description: Probiotic lactic acid bacteria strains isolated directly from traditional Graviera (ACA-DC 2640 and ACA-DC 4039); adhere to human gut epithelial cells; upregulate anti-inflammatory IL-10; produce ACE-inhibitory metabolites in cell-based studies

name: Thymol
description: Phenolic monoterpene derived from Thymus plant nectar; primary marker compound of thyme honey; disrupts bacterial cell membrane integrity and inhibits biofilm formation (S. aureus inhibition up to 80%); key driver of thyme honey's antimicrobial activity and exceptionally high total phenolic content (up to 193 mg/100g — among the highest recorded for any honey variety)

name: Kaempferol
description: Flavonol polyphenol transferred into honey from Thymus plant origin; anti-inflammatory and antioxidant; contributes to thyme honey's mucosal-protective properties and high DPPH radical-scavenging capacity (IC50 15.37 mg/mL)

name: Cichoric acid
description: Primary phenolic acid of Cichorium spinosum (dicaffeoyl tartaric acid); strongest antioxidant compound in traditional stamnagathi decoctions; significantly reduces intracellular ROS in human cells; DPPH IC50 ~15 μg/mL; the defining phytochemical marker of the Cretan stamnagathi decoction

name: Caftaric acid
description: Second major phenolic acid in stamnagathi decoctions (caffeoyl tartaric acid); strong free-radical scavenging activity; identified alongside cichoric acid as a primary antioxidant in Cretan C. spinosum; contributes to the vascular-protective polyphenol profile

name: 8-Deacetylmatricarin-8-O-sulphate (Cretan sesquiterpene lactone)
description: Sulfoconjugate sesquiterpene lactone isolated exclusively from Cretan Cichorium spinosum — not found in C. intybus or other chicory varieties; represents a chemotaxonomic marker unique to the Cretan species; class of sesquiterpene lactones (including lactupicrin) associated with anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective biological activity

name: Carvacrol
description: Phenolic monoterpene comprising 52.2% of dittany essential oil; primary antimicrobial driver — disrupts bacterial cell membranes against S. aureus, E. coli, Listeria, and Salmonella; potent DPPH antioxidant (IC50 0.045% v/v); responsible for the characteristic warm, spicy aroma; also inhibits acetylcholinesterase and interacts with alpha-glucosidase active site (molecular docking)

name: Rosmarinic acid
description: Major polyphenolic ester in dittany polar extracts; strong anti-inflammatory and antioxidant; inhibits COX enzymes and NF-kB pathways; dominant polar phenolic alongside the novel benzodioxane depside salvianolic acid P (first isolated from dittany)

name: Apigenin
description: Flavonoid isolated from dittany; inhibits acetylcholinesterase (AChE) in vitro — an enzyme whose excess activity is associated with Alzheimer's disease; anti-inflammatory and antioxidant

name: Novel luteolin/apigenin glycosides
description: Four novel flavone glycosides described for the first time in O. dictamnus infusion (Paloukopoulou 2026) including luteolin-7-O-[caffeoylglucuronyl]-glucuronopyranoside; structurally unique to dittany; contribute to the spasmolytic gut motility activity observed in ex vivo intestinal model

name: Galactomannans (locust bean gum)
description: Soluble dietary fibre comprising ~75% of carob seed endosperm; viscous in solution — slows gastric emptying and cholesterol absorption; fermented by gut bacteria to produce short-chain fatty acids; responsible for the satiety and glycaemic-moderating effects of carob

name: D-pinitol
description: Unique cyclitol compound (3-O-methyl-D-chiro-inositol) abundant in carob pulp; acts as an insulin sensitiser — enhances glucose uptake into cells via insulin-independent pathways; one of the proposed mechanisms for carob's ability to reduce postprandial glucose response and support metabolic health

name: Condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins)
description: Polyphenolic compounds responsible for carob's cholesterol-lowering effects; bind bile acids in the gut, reducing their reabsorption and forcing the liver to convert more LDL cholesterol into bile acids — the same mechanism as cholestyramine; also antioxidant and anti-inflammatory

name: Quercetin and myricetin
description: Flavonol polyphenols in carob pods and leaves; antioxidant and cardioprotective; contribute to carob's overall polyphenol content alongside gallic acid and ellagic acid

name: Punicalagins
description: Largest-molecular-weight ellagitannins found in pomegranate peel and juice; hydrolysed in the gut to ellagic acid then metabolised by gut bacteria to urolithins; responsible for pomegranate's exceptional antioxidant capacity — demonstrated to exceed both red wine and green tea by standardised ORAC assay; the key compounds driving anti-inflammatory and vascular effects observed in clinical trials

name: Anthocyanins (delphinidin
description: cyanidin
column6: Polyphenolic pigments concentrated in pomegranate arils and juice; produce the characteristic deep red colour; anti-inflammatory via NF-κB pathway suppression; inhibit ICAM-1 and IL-6 expression — matching the biomarkers improved in the 2025 meta-analysis of 19 clinical trials; also antioxidant and cardioprotective

name: Punicic acid (Omega-5 fatty acid)
description: Unusual conjugated linolenic acid (18:3 cis-9 trans-11 cis-13) present in pomegranate seed oil; a structural isomer of conjugated linolenic acid; anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative properties; acts via PPAR-gamma activation to modulate lipid metabolism

name: Cynarin (1
description: 5-dicaffeoylquinic acid)
column5: The signature bitter phenolic of artichoke; directly stimulates bile secretion from the liver and gallbladder; bile acid export lowers hepatic cholesterol pools — the mechanism by which artichoke leaf extract reduces LDL in humans; responsible for the distinctive flavour and the post-artichoke sweet-water perception

name: Chlorogenic acid
description: Hydroxycinnamic acid polyphenol abundant in artichoke leaves and bracts; antioxidant and anti-inflammatory; inhibits glucose-6-phosphatase in the liver — reduces hepatic glucose output; also found in high concentrations in green coffee

name: Inulin (fructooligosaccharides)
description: Prebiotic soluble fibre comprising the storage carbohydrate of artichoke; selectively feeds Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus species; fermented to butyrate and SCFAs in the colon; improves bowel transit and supports the gut epithelial barrier

name: Oleuropein
description: The dominant bitter secoiridoid glycoside in olive leaves; present at 60-90 mg/g dry leaf weight — 10-20x higher than in olive oil; ACE-inhibitory activity lowers blood pressure; antioxidant; hydrolysed in the body to hydroxytyrosol and elenolic acid; the primary compound responsible for antihypertensive effects demonstrated in human crossover RCTs

name: Hydroxytyrosol
description: One of the most potent plant-derived antioxidants known; anti-inflammatory via NF-κB and COX-2 suppression; found in olive leaves at higher concentrations than in EVOO; metabolite of oleuropein; contributes to lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory effects of olive leaf extract observed in clinical trials

name: Beta-glucan (barley)
description: Viscous soluble dietary fibre comprising 3-11% of whole-grain barley by weight; forms a thick gel in the small intestine that traps bile acids, preventing their reabsorption and forcing the liver to convert LDL cholesterol into replacement bile acids; this mechanism earned an FDA-approved cardiovascular health claim; a 50g serving of Cretan paximadi provides approximately 2-3g beta-glucan

name: Arabinoxylan
description: Insoluble prebiotic fibre comprising the cell walls of barley bran; fermented by colonic bacteria to produce butyrate, propionate, and acetate; butyrate is the preferred energy substrate of colonocytes; supports colon health, reduces intestinal inflammation, and improves insulin sensitivity via SCFA signalling

name: Hydroxytyrosol (free form)
description: The primary phenolic antioxidant in table olives present at 8-fold higher concentration per gram than in extra virgin olive oil; the fermentation and curing process hydrolyses oleuropein glucoside into free hydroxytyrosol; demonstrated to be bioavailable in humans — plasma levels peak within 30 minutes of olive consumption; inhibits LDL oxidation, platelet aggregation, and endothelial inflammation via NF-κB; the same compound responsible for the cardiovascular benefits documented in the PREDIMED trial

name: Oleuropein glucoside and its aglycone
description: The intact precursor compound of hydroxytyrosol present in fresh uncured olives; provides characteristic extreme bitterness of raw olives before curing; the curing process hydrolyses the glucoside bond and further breaks down oleuropein aglycone to release free hydroxytyrosol and elenolic acid; different curing methods (brine vs dry salt vs lye) produce different polyphenol profiles; naturally cured Greek-style olives retain higher total polyphenol content than commercially processed varieties

name: Tyrosol
description: Secondary olive phenolic co-occurring with hydroxytyrosol throughout the Olea europaea plant; weaker antioxidant than HT but present at significant quantities in both olive oil and table olives; both HT and tyrosol are consistently detectable in human plasma after olive consumption in pharmacokinetic studies; anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet activity in vitro; contributes additively to the overall phenolic protection of the olive polyphenol matrix

name: Lactobacillus acidophilus and L. bulgaricus (live cultures)
description: The active therapeutic agents in traditionally fermented yoghurt; L. acidophilus produces bile salt hydrolase (BSH) — the enzyme that deconjugates bile acids in the gut, forcing the liver to synthesise replacement bile acids from circulating LDL cholesterol, directly lowering LDL; L. bulgaricus produces lactic acid and bacteriocins; both strains survive gastric transit in yoghurt matrix better than in capsule form; the live probiotic count at consumption is the primary determinant of cholesterol-lowering efficacy

name: Casein-derived ACE-inhibitory peptides (Val-Pro-Pro; Ile-Pro-Pro)
description: Bioactive tripeptides released during fermentation of sheep and goat casein by lactic acid bacteria; competitively inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) — the same enzyme targeted by prescription ACE-inhibitor antihypertensive drugs (ramipril, lisinopril); blood pressure reduction from fermented dairy consumption in human trials is partially attributed to these peptides; sheep and goat milk casein yields higher ACE-inhibitory peptide concentrations than cow casein due to different protein composition

name: Carvacrol
description: The dominant phenolic monoterpenoid in Satureja thymbra essential oil (40-70% of oil); identical compound to the primary bioactive in Origanum and other Cretan medicinal herbs; the active agent responsible for the metabolic effects seen in the Satureja khuzestanica RCT (FBS reduction, HbA1c improvement, lipid normalisation); inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) reducing prostaglandin synthesis; strong antimicrobial membrane disruptor active against MRSA and enteric pathogens

name: Rosmarinic acid
description: Polyphenol ester abundant in all Lamiaceae family herbs including savory, oregano, dittany, rosemary, and basil; potent antioxidant with ORAC value exceeding vitamin C; inhibits complement system C3 convertase activation and 5-lipoxygenase, reducing both inflammatory cascade activation and leukotriene synthesis; well-studied in in vitro models; European Medicines Agency has accepted rosmarinic acid content as a quality marker for medicinal Lamiaceae herbs

name: Thymol
description: Phenolic monoterpenoid co-occurring with carvacrol; same compound dominant in thyme; antimicrobial membrane disruptor particularly effective against biofilm-forming bacteria; exhibits HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity in mechanistic studies (same molecular target as statin drugs); the combination of carvacrol and thymol shows synergistic antimicrobial activity greater than either compound alone — the natural ratio in Satureja essential oil is likely more effective than isolated compounds

name: Carvacrol
description: The dominant phenolic monoterpenoid in Origanum vulgare essential oil, comprising 60-80% of Cretan wild oregano oil; Greek wild oregano contains among the highest carvacrol concentrations documented globally — Cretan rigani is prized partly for this potency; identical bioactive compound found in Cretan dittany and savory; inhibits COX-1, COX-2, NF-κB, and LPS-induced cytokine release; potent broad-spectrum antimicrobial disrupting bacterial cell membrane integrity; EFSA has noted carvacrol as a flavouring with documented biological activity

name: Rosmarinic acid
description: Polyphenol ester at 10-20 mg/g dry weight in Origanum vulgare — higher than in rosemary despite the name; potent antioxidant (3x more potent than vitamin C by DPPH assay); inhibits complement C3 convertase activation and 5-lipoxygenase, reducing both complement-mediated and leukotriene-mediated inflammation; European Medicines Agency uses rosmarinic acid content as a quality marker for medicinal Lamiaceae preparations; anti-inflammatory mechanism relevant to atherosclerosis, arthritis, and neuroinflammation

name: Trans-anethole
description: The primary volatile compound in fennel essential oil (60-80%); responsible for the characteristic anise flavour; primary spasmolytic agent — relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle by inhibiting calcium-mediated and serotonin-mediated contractions; demonstrated carminative (gas-relieving) activity by reducing intestinal motility and intraluminal pressure; mild estrogenic activity at high doses (relevant to traditional use for menstrual regulation); anti-inflammatory activity via NF-κB suppression; the spasmolytic mechanism explains why both traditional fennel seed tea and the clinical RCT results converge on gut comfort benefits

name: Fenchone and fenchyl alcohol
description: Secondary monoterpenoids contributing 10-20% of fennel essential oil; fenchone has documented expectorant, antimicrobial, and antifungal properties; FAAH (fatty acid amide hydrolase) inhibitory activity — FAAH degrades endocannabinoids, so its inhibition extends endocannabinoid signalling, which contributes to GI motility regulation and pain reduction; fenchyl alcohol demonstrates additional spasmolytic activity synergistic with trans-anethole; the combination of trans-anethole and fenchone in whole fennel oil is more effective than isolated anethole, consistent with whole-herb traditional use

name: Masticadienonic acid
description: Pentacyclic triterpenic acid characteristic of Pistacia lentiscus var. chia (Chios mastic); one of the dominant bioactive triterpenoids in mastic gum responsible for the documented effects on gastrointestinal motility and mucosal protection; mechanism: inhibits gastric H+/K+-ATPase activity and modulates intestinal smooth muscle contractility; serves as a chemotaxonomic marker for authentic Chios-variant mastic

name: Isomasticadienonic acid
description: Isomer of masticadienonic acid co-occurring in Pistacia lentiscus resin; contributes to the overall triterpenoid profile responsible for mastics prokinetic and anti-Helicobacter pylori activity demonstrated in clinical trials; the combination of masticadienonic acid and isomasticadienonic acid distinguishes Chios mastic from other Pistacia lentiscus varieties

name: Alpha-pinene
description: Bicyclic monoterpene comprising 50-80% of mastic essential oil — responsible for the characteristic pine-resinous aroma; potent antimicrobial against oral pathogens (S. mutans, P. gingivalis) and gastric pathogens (H. pylori) at concentrations achieved through mastic consumption; partly volatilises during cooking but is retained in chewed mastic gum and in distilled mastichi liqueur

name: Beta-myrcene and other monoterpenes
description: Volatile monoterpene fraction of mastic essential oil (10-20%); contributes additional antimicrobial activity and may modulate gastrointestinal motility through TRP channel interactions; the whole essential oil matrix appears to be more effective than isolated alpha-pinene alone, suggesting synergistic activity consistent with traditional whole-resin consumption rather than isolated compound supplementation

name: Rutin (quercetin-3-O-rutinoside)
description: Quercetin glycoside present in caper fruit and buds at among the highest concentrations documented in any vegetable food (170-330 mg/100g in fresh capers); rutin is hydrolysed by gut bacteria to quercetin, which inhibits alpha-glucosidase (lowering post-prandial glucose), aldose reductase (reducing diabetic complications), and ACE (lowering blood pressure); rutin specifically also has direct antithrombotic activity and microvascular protective effects

name: Quercetin
description: Aglycone flavonol released from caper rutin by intestinal hydrolysis; one of the most extensively studied dietary polyphenols globally; in capers, quercetin occurs both as the glycoside (rutin) and in free form; inhibits ACE (blood pressure reduction), HMG-CoA reductase (cholesterol lowering), and platelet thromboxane synthesis; quercetin from capers complements the quercetin already provided by Cretan onions and contributes to the overall flavonol load of traditional Cretan cuisine

name: Kaempferol and stachydrine
description: Kaempferol is the second major flavonol in caper (~50-100 mg/100g) with anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet activity; stachydrine is a quaternary ammonium alkaloid unique to capers and a few other Capparidaceae plants that contributes to the bitter-pungent flavour and shows modest anti-inflammatory and cardioprotective activity in animal models; the multi-compound profile of capers makes them one of the more flavonoid-dense vegetables in the Mediterranean diet

name: Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA)
description: Plant omega-3 fatty acid (18:3 n-3) comprising 9-14% of walnut fat — the highest concentration among commonly consumed nuts; the body converts a fraction of ALA to EPA and DHA, providing cardiovascular benefits without consuming fish; ALA itself reduces LDL oxidation, modulates inflammatory cytokine production, and improves endothelial function as measured by flow-mediated dilation; walnut ALA is the primary mechanism behind the documented FMD improvement in pre-diabetic and metabolic syndrome populations

name: Gamma-tocopherol
description: Less famous than alpha-tocopherol but more abundant in walnuts; gamma-tocopherol specifically traps reactive nitrogen species (peroxynitrite) that alpha-tocopherol cannot — a complementary antioxidant activity; walnut contains 5-10x more gamma-tocopherol than most other nuts; serum gamma-tocopherol levels are inversely associated with cardiovascular risk in prospective cohort data; the walnut tocopherol mix is one of the few dietary sources delivering meaningful gamma-tocopherol

name: Ellagic acid and ellagitannins
description: Polyphenols abundant in walnut pellicle (the brown skin); metabolised by gut bacteria to urolithins — the same secondary metabolites produced from pomegranate punicalagins; urolithin A has been shown to activate mitophagy (the cellular recycling of dysfunctional mitochondria) and is associated with improved muscle function in older adults; walnut and pomegranate provide overlapping urolithin precursor pools in the traditional Cretan diet

name: Walnut melatonin
description: Walnuts contain dietary melatonin at 3-4 ng/g — among the higher concentrations in nuts; consuming walnuts has been documented to raise serum melatonin in human pharmacokinetic studies; when combined with the omega-3 content, walnuts deliver both a circadian signal and the neuro-supportive fatty acid substrate; complements the dietary melatonin available from Cretan tomatoes and purslane

name: Alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E)
description: Almonds contain 25-30 mg alpha-tocopherol per 100g — the richest plant source among commonly consumed foods; a 28g portion (one ounce) provides ~7 mg, nearly half the adult RDA; alpha-tocopherol inhibits LDL oxidation, a critical step in atherosclerosis; the skin (brown outer layer) of almonds also contains polyphenols (catechins, epicatechin) that act synergistically with vitamin E to extend the lag phase of LDL oxidation

name: Oleic acid (MUFA)
description: Almond fat is dominated by oleic acid — the same monounsaturated fatty acid that makes olive oil cardiovascular-protective; substituting dietary saturated fat with almond MUFA lowers LDL cholesterol without reducing protective HDL; this is the primary mechanism behind the consistent ~5-10 mg/dL LDL reductions documented across multiple almond meta-analyses; the oleic acid in almonds complements rather than duplicates the oleic acid from olive oil — almonds deliver this MUFA in a fibre + protein matrix that increases satiety

name: Magnesium and prebiotic fibre
description: Almonds provide 270 mg magnesium per 100g — among the highest dietary sources; magnesium is a cofactor for over 300 enzymatic reactions including those regulating blood pressure and insulin signalling; almond fibre (~12g per 100g, mostly insoluble) is fermented by colonic bacteria to short-chain fatty acids and acts as a prebiotic, modulating gut microbiota composition in human trials; the magnesium + fibre + MUFA combination explains the body weight (−1.39 kg) and blood pressure improvements observed in the Lee-Bravatti 2019 meta-analysis

name: Carnosic acid and carnosol
description: Carnosic acid is the dominant diterpene phenolic in Salvia fruticosa and the related Mediterranean sages; oxidises to carnosol in plant tissue and during storage; both compounds are potent antioxidants and crystallographically documented to inhibit acetylcholinesterase (AChE) — the molecular target of prescription Alzheimers drugs (donepezil, rivastigmine); rosemary and sage are the richest dietary sources of carnosic acid; the same mechanism (AChE inhibition) explains the cognitive enhancement documented in the Wightman 2021 RCT and the Miroddi 2014 systematic review
8-Cineole (eucalyptol)
column5: Volatile monoterpenoid comprising 30-60% of Greek sage (Salvia fruticosa) essential oil — the chemotype that distinguishes Cretan faskomilo from Northern European Salvia officinalis (which is dominated by alpha-thujone); 1,8-cineole crosses the blood-brain barrier rapidly and inhibits both AChE and BuChE in vitro; serum 1,8-cineole concentrations correlate with cognitive performance in human pharmacokinetic studies of inhaled and oral eucalyptol exposure

name: Rosmarinic acid
description: Polyphenol ester present at high concentrations in all Mediterranean Lamiaceae herbs — sage, oregano, savory, dittany, rosemary, lemon balm; ORAC antioxidant value exceeding vitamin C; inhibits complement C3 convertase and 5-lipoxygenase, reducing both complement-mediated and leukotriene-mediated inflammation; in faskomilo specifically, rosmarinic acid contributes both to the cognitive support (via brain antioxidant protection) and to the traditional Cretan reputation of sage tea for cleansing the body

name: Terpenoids (gamma-terpinene & limonene)
description: Dominant volatile compounds in kritamo essential oil; gamma-terpinene and limonene show in vitro antibacterial, antifungal, anti-inflammatory, and 5-lipoxygenase inhibitory activity; responsible for the herb's characteristic aroma.

name: Chlorogenic acid & flavonoids (rutin & hyperoside)
description: Hydroxycinnamic acid and flavonoid glycosides characterised by LC-DAD-HRMS in kritamo sprouts; chlorogenic acid is the dominant phenolic; rutin and hyperoside provide antioxidant and potential anti-inflammatory activity via free-radical scavenging.

name: Omega-3 & omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids
description: Kritamo leaves are a source of linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3) from a coastal wild plant; fatty acid profile supports anti-inflammatory potential and complements the broader Mediterranean omega-3 context.

name: Anthocyanins (cyanidin-3-rutinoside)
description: Primary pigment in dark-skinned Cretan figs; potent free-radical scavenger and NF-κB inhibitor; in vitro studies show anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer properties; cyanidin-3-rutinoside is the dominant anthocyanin in Ficus carica skin.

name: Rutin & chlorogenic acid
description: Rutin (quercetin-3-rutinoside) and chlorogenic acid are the dominant phenolic compounds in fig flesh; both are well-characterised antioxidants with in vitro alpha-glucosidase inhibition (anti-diabetic mechanism) and cholinesterase inhibition (neuroprotective mechanism).

name: Dietary fibre (soluble & insoluble)
description: Fresh and dried figs are among the highest-fibre fruits; soluble fibre (pectin) slows glucose absorption and lowers LDL; insoluble fibre supports gut motility; drying concentrates the fibre content, making dried Cretan syka a practical fibre delivery vehicle.

name: Omega-3 & omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids (balanced ratio)
description: Snail flesh contains a favourable omega-3 to omega-6 ratio with predominantly unsaturated fatty acids; the PUFA profile is comparable in structure to that of oily fish; supports anti-inflammatory and cardiovascular-protective mechanisms.

name: Complete protein (all essential amino acids)
description: Helix aspersa flesh provides all essential amino acids at nutritionally meaningful concentrations; high biological value protein comparable to conventional animal protein sources; particularly notable given the very low calorie density (~77 kcal per 100g).

name: Antioxidant biomolecules (flesh extracts)
description: Extracts of H. aspersa flesh contain a large quantity of antioxidant biomolecules with significant free-radical scavenging activity; specific compounds include phenolics and other small molecules as yet uncharacterised; activity confirmed by DPPH assay.

name: Quercetin glycosides (rutin, isoquercitrin)
description: The dominant flavonoid family in red vine leaves; strengthen capillary walls, reduce vascular permeability, and inhibit leukocyte adhesion to vein endothelium — the mechanism behind documented reductions in leg edema in chronic venous insufficiency trials.

name: Resveratrol
description: Stilbene polyphenol present in vine leaves; activates SIRT1 and AMPK pathways linked to mitochondrial biogenesis, vascular endothelial protection, and cellular longevity.

name: Kaempferol
description: Flavonoid present alongside quercetin in vine leaves; well-documented anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity via inhibition of NF-κB signalling and direct ROS scavenging.

name: Caffeic acid
description: Hydroxycinnamic acid abundant in vine leaves; potent free radical scavenger and inhibitor of LDL oxidation; one of the most studied dietary polyphenols for cardiovascular protection.

name: Thymol
description: Phenolic monoterpene; 10-64% of thyme essential oil; documented antimicrobial, expectorant, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory activity across in vitro, animal, and clinical studies; the long-standing active in traditional thyme cough syrups.

name: Carvacrol
description: Phenolic monoterpene isomer of thymol; particularly concentrated in Greek thyme (Coridothymus capitatus); shares with thymol broad antimicrobial activity and modulation of TRPV3 ion channels involved in inflammation and pain signalling.

name: p-Cymene
description: Aromatic monoterpene present alongside thymol and carvacrol in thyme essential oil; acts synergistically with thymol to enhance antimicrobial activity and cell-membrane penetration.

name: Rosmarinic acid
description: Polyphenol present in thyme leaves; potent antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compound shared with other Lamiaceae herbs including oregano, sage, and dittany.

name: Sodium chloride
description: The dominant constituent of sea salt (~95-98% by weight); essential dietary mineral, but excessive intake is one of the most consistently documented dietary risk factors for hypertension, stroke, and cardiovascular mortality.

name: Magnesium chloride / sulfate
description: Naturally present in unrefined sea salt at trace concentrations (~0.5-1%); contributes to the slightly bitter mineral edge of unrefined salts; dietary magnesium itself is beneficial but the amount delivered via salt is small.

name: Trace minerals (calcium, potassium)
description: Present in unrefined sea salt at very low concentrations (<1% combined); contribute to mineral content but in amounts too small to be nutritionally meaningful at typical culinary use.

name: Whey bioactive peptides
description: Short protein fragments released during digestion of whey cheese; include ACE-inhibitory and immune-modulating sequences; documented across cheese category evidence (Zhang 2023 umbrella review; Zhuang 2025 cohort analysis).

name: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)
description: Natural trans-fatty acid concentrated in pasture-fed sheep and goat dairy; anti-inflammatory and potentially antiatherogenic; higher in traditional Cretan whey cheese than in commercial cow-milk dairy.

name: Whey protein (alpha-lactalbumin, beta-lactoglobulin)
description: Complete protein with all essential amino acids and high branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) content; supports lean muscle mass and satiety; rapidly digested.

name: Whey bioactive peptides
description: Released from whey proteins during digestion; share ACE-inhibitory and immune-modulating activity documented in cheese-category cohort studies.

name: Calcium and short-chain fatty acids
description: Dense in dietary calcium per gram and contains short-chain fatty acids from sheep and goat butterfat; supports bone density and gut epithelial energy supply.

name: Conjugated Linoleic Acid (CLA)
description: A naturally occurring fatty acid found in sheep and goat milk fat; associated in preclinical studies with reduced adiposity and anti-inflammatory signalling.

name: Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB)
description: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum and Lacticaseibacillus paracasei strains characterised in Greek feta-type cheese; assessed for cholesterol assimilation, alpha-glucosidase inhibition, and gut epithelial adhesion in vitro.

name: Calcium & Whey Peptides
description: Feta is a significant source of bioavailable calcium; its whey fraction contains short peptides with documented ACE-inhibitory potential linked to blood pressure modulation.

name: EPA (Eicosapentaenoic Acid)
description: A long-chain omega-3 fatty acid abundantly supplied by sardines and anchovies; reduces triglycerides, inhibits platelet aggregation, and suppresses inflammatory eicosanoid production.

name: DHA (Docosahexaenoic Acid)
description: Essential for brain structure and retinal function; found in high concentrations in small oily fish; cardiovascular-protective through multiple lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory mechanisms.

name: Coenzyme Q10 & Selenium
description: Sardines are among the richest dietary sources of CoQ10 (mitochondrial antioxidant) and bioavailable selenium, both supporting cardiovascular function and longevity outcomes.

name: Taurine
description: A sulphur-containing amino acid found in especially high concentrations in octopus and cephalopods; supports cardiovascular function, bile acid conjugation, and antioxidant defence.

name: Selenium & Zinc
description: Octopus is a rich source of both trace minerals — selenium supports thyroid function and glutathione peroxidase antioxidant activity; zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

name: Lean Protein
description: Octopus provides approximately 15g protein per 100g cooked weight with very low fat content (~1g), making it one of the highest protein-to-calorie-ratio seafoods available.

name: Omega-3 Fatty Acids (EPA & DHA)
description: Both Sparus aurata and Dicentrarchus labrax deliver significant long-chain omega-3 fatty acids supporting cardiovascular, cognitive, and visual health under EU-authorised health claims.

name: Selenium & Phosphorus
description: High selenium content supports antioxidant enzyme systems; phosphorus is essential for bone mineralisation and ATP-based cellular energy metabolism.

name: Complete Protein
description: Sea bream and sea bass provide high biological value protein containing all essential amino acids; their amino acid profile meets EU criteria for authorised protein nutrition claims.

name: Safranal
description: The primary volatile compound responsible for saffron's aroma; exerts anxiolytic and antidepressant effects via serotonin reuptake inhibition and GABA-A receptor modulation.

name: Crocin & Crocetin
description: Carotenoid glycosides responsible for saffron's deep colour; studied for neuroprotective, antidepressant, and cognitive-enhancing effects across multiple human RCTs.

name: Kaempferol
description: A flavonoid in saffron petals with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties; contributes to the compound's overall neuroprotective profile.

name: Polyphenols & Flavonoids
description: Pine honey has a distinct phenolic profile from floral honeys; total phenolic content ~451 mg GAE/kg; FRAP antioxidant values higher than most European monofloral honeys.

name: Hydrogen Peroxide & Defensin-1
description: Key antibacterial agents in pine honey; activity against nosocomial and foodborne pathogens — in Greek studies comparable or superior to Manuka honey for some strains.

name: Oligosaccharides & Minerals
description: Honeydew honeys are rich in oligosaccharides with prebiotic potential, and have higher mineral content (potassium, calcium, magnesium) than nectar honeys.

name: Resistant Starch & Soluble Fibre
description: Black-eyed peas have a low glycemic index; their resistant starch and soluble fibre slow glucose absorption, blunt postprandial insulin response, and promote satiety.

name: Plant Protein & Iron
description: Vigna unguiculata provides ~24g protein per 100g dry weight with a favourable amino acid profile; a good plant-based iron source especially for low-meat diets.

name: Polyphenols (Vitexin, Isovitexin)
description: Black-eyed peas contain flavone C-glycosides with documented NF-κB pathway inhibition and antioxidant activity; contribute to anti-inflammatory properties.

name: Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB)
description: Sour trahanas is fermented with naturally occurring LAB — predominantly Lactobacillus and Streptococcus species — that acidify the mixture and survive partial drying. Related strains in Greek dairy fermentations (feta, yoghurt) have been documented for probiotic properties including gut epithelial adhesion and cholesterol assimilation.

name: Fermented Wheat Proteins & Bioactive Peptides
description: Fermentation of wheat with acidified milk partially pre-digests gluten proteins and generates bioactive peptides with documented ACE-inhibitory potential, improving digestibility compared to unfermented grain products.

name: Complex Carbohydrates & Resistant Starch
description: Cracked wheat base provides slow-release complex carbohydrates; the fermentation and drying process increases resistant starch content, supporting lower glycemic response compared to refined grain products.

name: Resistant Starch & Beta-Glucans
description: Chickpeas contain resistant starch and beta-glucan soluble fibre that resists digestion in the small intestine, reaching the colon where it is fermented by microbiota. This slow fermentation produces short-chain fatty acids that blunt postprandial glucose spikes and improve insulin sensitivity, explaining the significant glycaemic-lowering effect observed in meta-analyses of controlled trials (postprandial glucose iAUC -47.89; p<0.0001).

name: Isoflavones & Polyphenols
description: Chickpeas are among the richest non-soy sources of isoflavones (biochanin A, formononetin) and polyphenols including ferulic acid and kaempferol. These phytoestrogens and antioxidant phenolics reduce LDL oxidation and support cardiovascular health, particularly relevant in postmenopausal populations.

name: Plant Protein & Essential Amino Acids
description: Chickpeas provide 19-20g protein per 100g dry weight including lysine (often limiting in cereals). The protein-fibre combination slows gastric emptying, contributing to the low glycaemic index (~28-35) and documented satiety effect of chickpea consumption.

name: Resveratrol
description: Resveratrol is a stilbene polyphenol found predominantly in grape skins. A 2026 meta-analysis of 40 RCTs (2551 participants) found resveratrol supplementation significantly reduced HOMA-IR, total cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides, blood pressure, hs-CRP, TNF-alpha, and IL-6. Mechanisms include SIRT1 activation, eNOS upregulation (nitric oxide production), and NF-kB suppression.

name: Quercetin & Flavonols
description: Cretan grapes contain high levels of quercetin and kaempferol glycosides, concentrated in the skin and seeds. Quercetin inhibits LDL oxidation, reduces platelet aggregation, and modulates histamine release. Its bioavailability is enhanced by the co-presence of resveratrol and catechin in whole grapes and grape products.

name: Oligomeric Proanthocyanidins (OPCs)
description: Grape seeds and skins are among the richest sources of oligomeric proanthocyanidins (condensed tannins) — powerful vascular antioxidants that bind to collagen and elastin in vessel walls, strengthening capillary integrity and improving circulation. Cretan sun-dried grapes (raisins) concentrate these compounds.

name: Betacyanins & Betalains
description: Prickly pear derives its colour from betacyanins and betaxanthins — nitrogen-containing pigments unique to the order Caryophyllales. Unlike anthocyanins, betalains are highly bioavailable. A 2025 clinical trial documented 48% increase in total antioxidant capacity and 59.8% reduction in 8-OHdG (DNA oxidative damage marker) after 3 months in healthy adults.

name: Indicaxanthin
description: Indicaxanthin is a betaxanthin unique to Opuntia ficus-indica with particularly strong free-radical scavenging activity in vitro and ex vivo. Unlike many dietary antioxidants, it retains activity in the oxidative conditions of the gut. Human pharmacokinetic studies confirm its absorption and accumulation in plasma after fruit consumption.

name: Vitamin C & Polyphenols
description: Prickly pear contains 22-35mg/100g vitamin C alongside quercetin, isorhamnetin, and kaempferol glycosides. These water-soluble antioxidants act synergistically with betalain pigments, providing protection against oxidative stress through complementary mechanisms across both aqueous and lipid cellular compartments.

name: Rosmarinic Acid
description: Rosmarinic acid is a polyphenolic ester found at high concentrations in spearmint. The extract studied in cognitive RCTs is standardised to a minimum 14.5% rosmarinic acid. It inhibits acetylcholinesterase and monoamine oxidase, supporting cholinergic neurotransmission and noradrenaline availability — mechanisms relevant to attention and working memory improvements documented in clinical trials.

name: Carvone & Flavonoid Complex
description: L-carvone is the principal monoterpene responsible for spearmint's characteristic aroma and biological activity. In vitro studies show carvone modulates GABA-A receptors and voltage-gated calcium channels. Combined with luteolin, apigenin, and hesperidin in spearmint leaf, this flavonoid complex may contribute to mild anxiolytic and sleep-facilitating effects observed alongside cognitive improvements in clinical trials.

name: Limonene & Terpene Antioxidants
description: Spearmint essential oil contains limonene, beta-pinene, and dihydrocarvone alongside carvone. These terpene antioxidants have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties in cell models; spearmint leaf extract inhibits lipid peroxidation and scavenges hydroxyl radicals — contributing to neuroprotection during ageing.

name: Lutein & Zeaxanthin
description: Pistachios are the richest nut source of lutein and zeaxanthin — xanthophyll carotenoids that concentrate in the retinal macula and provide oxidative protection against age-related macular degeneration. These carotenoids also act as systemic antioxidants and may contribute to the anti-inflammatory activity observed in pistachio trials.

name: Gamma-Tocopherol
description: Pistachios contain gamma-tocopherol as their primary vitamin E form — distinct from the alpha-tocopherol in most supplements. Gamma-tocopherol has unique anti-inflammatory properties, neutralising reactive nitrogen species. This form has been associated with reduced endothelial inflammation and plaque formation in cardiovascular disease models.

name: Arginine & Phytosterols
description: Pistachios are among the richest nut sources of arginine — the amino acid precursor to nitric oxide synthesis in vascular endothelium. Increased nitric oxide promotes vasodilation and is a key mechanism behind the blood pressure-lowering effect documented in 13 RCTs. Pistachio phytosterols (beta-sitosterol, campesterol) additionally compete with dietary cholesterol for absorption.

name: Folate & B-Vitamins
description: Lentils are one of the richest sources of folate (vitamin B9), providing ~358ug per 100g cooked — nearly the entire recommended daily intake. Folate is required for homocysteine remethylation; elevated homocysteine is an independent cardiovascular risk factor. Lentils also provide thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6.

name: Slow-Release Carbohydrates & Resistant Starch
description: Lentils have a glycaemic index of 29-35 — one of the lowest of any carbohydrate food. Their resistant starch and soluble fibre slows glucose absorption, reduces postprandial insulin response, and promotes butyrate production by colonic microbiota. Meta-analyses of legume RCTs confirm reductions in fasting glucose and HOMA-IR.

name: Polyphenols & Tannins
description: Lentil seed coats are rich in condensed tannins, ferulic acid, catechin, and procyanidins. These polyphenols inhibit alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase (slowing starch digestion), chelate LDL-oxidising metals, and reduce intestinal cholesterol absorption. Black and green lentils have higher polyphenol concentrations than red varieties.

name: Sesamin & Sesamolin
description: Sesamin and sesamolin are fat-soluble lignans unique to sesame. They are converted by gut microbiota to enterolactone and enterodiol — mammalian lignans with documented effects on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation via eNOS pathway, and inhibition of delta-5 desaturase (reducing arachidonic acid production and thereby inflammation).

name: Sesaminol & Antioxidant Lignans
description: Sesaminol is formed from sesame lignans during roasting (the tahini process) and is a potent antioxidant protecting against LDL oxidation. The combined lignan complex has demonstrated blood pressure-lowering, cholesterol-lowering, and anti-inflammatory properties in clinical trials, including an RCT in 300 hypertensive patients where sesame oil as sole cooking oil for 60 days improved all cardiovascular risk markers.

name: Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids (PUFA)
description: Sesame oil is ~41% linoleic acid (omega-6) and ~39% oleic acid (omega-9), giving a fatty acid profile intermediate between sunflower and olive oil. While the omega-6:3 ratio is not ideal, the lignan content uniquely counteracts the pro-inflammatory tendency of omega-6 fats — distinguishing sesame's cardiovascular effects from other high-PUFA oils.

name: Lycopene
description: Lycopene is a fat-soluble carotenoid responsible for the red colour of ripe tomatoes and one of the most potent dietary antioxidants. An umbrella review of 17 meta-analyses found dietary lycopene intake inversely associated with all-cause mortality, stroke, CVD, metabolic syndrome, and prostate cancer. Bioavailability increases dramatically when tomatoes are cooked and eaten with oil.

name: Beta-Carotene & Carotenoid Complex
description: Beyond lycopene, tomatoes contain beta-carotene, phytoene, phytofluene, and beta-cryptoxanthin — carotenoids acting synergistically to protect vascular endothelium and skin from oxidative damage. Beta-carotene converts to vitamin A as needed; non-provitamin carotenoids function primarily as antioxidants and inflammation modulators.

name: Vitamin C & Potassium
description: A medium tomato provides 15-25mg vitamin C and ~300mg potassium. Potassium is directly inversely associated with blood pressure (promotes sodium excretion via the kidney) and is a key nutrient in the Cretan diet's documented cardioprotective effect. Combined with lycopene's LDL-antioxidant activity, tomato's micronutrient profile makes it a central pillar of Mediterranean cardiovascular protection.

name: Carnosic Acid
description: Carnosic acid is a diterpenoid phenol found at 4-8% dry weight in rosemary that acts as both a direct antioxidant and precursor to other bioactive compounds. In the brain, it activates the Nrf2 pathway — the master antioxidant transcription factor — protecting neurons from oxidative damage. It also inhibits acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that degrades acetylcholine (the neurotransmitter of attention, learning, and memory).

name: Carnosol
description: Carnosol is formed from carnosic acid during rosemary drying and processing, sharing similar neuroprotective properties. It has documented anti-inflammatory activity via NF-kB inhibition, antioxidant activity via multiple mechanisms, and has been studied for potential roles in cancer prevention. Carnosol's lipophilicity allows it to cross the blood-brain barrier.

name: Ursolic Acid
description: Ursolic acid is a pentacyclic triterpenoid found in rosemary's waxy leaf coating. It inhibits multiple neurodegeneration targets including acetylcholinesterase, beta-secretase (BACE-1), and inflammatory cyclooxygenase enzymes. The rosemary water RCT (Moss 2018) proposed both cholinergic and cerebrovascular mechanisms to explain the cognitive improvements observed after acute ingestion.

name: Pectin (Soluble Fibre)
description: Quince is one of the richest fruit sources of pectin — a soluble fibre that forms a viscous gel in the gut, slowing glucose absorption and binding bile acids (forcing the liver to divert cholesterol to bile acid synthesis, thereby lowering circulating LDL). Quince pectin has prebiotic properties, supporting beneficial gut bacteria in vitro and animal models.

name: Chlorogenic Acid
description: Chlorogenic acid is among the most abundant polyphenols in quince flesh. It inhibits glucose-6-phosphate translocase (reducing hepatic glucose output), has antihypertensive properties via eNOS activation, and demonstrates strong antioxidant activity in plasma. These mechanisms are consistent with the glycaemic and lipid improvements observed in the quince nutraceutical trial (Sardelli 2025).

name: Quercetin Glycosides
description: Quince skin is particularly rich in quercetin-3-glucoside and other flavonol glycosides with enhanced bioavailability compared to aglycone quercetin. These compounds have documented cardioprotective, anti-inflammatory, and antiviral properties. Quince's traditional use for sore throats and respiratory infections in Cretan folk medicine is consistent with the antimicrobial activity of quercetin and chlorogenic acid.

name: Nasunin (Anthocyanin)
description: Nasunin is an anthocyanin-type pigment unique to eggplant skin and one of the most potent antioxidants among common vegetables. It scavenges hydroxyl and peroxyl radicals, protects cell membrane lipids from peroxidation, and specifically protects mitochondrial lipids in neurons. Unlike many antioxidants, nasunin chelates iron and copper ions, preventing metal-catalysed oxidative reactions.

name: Chlorogenic Acid & Caffeic Acid
description: Eggplant flesh is among the richest vegetable sources of chlorogenic acid (responsible for its browning when cut). Along with caffeic acid, these hydroxycinnamate polyphenols inhibit alpha-glucosidase (slowing starch digestion), reduce LDL oxidation, and have hepatoprotective properties. Coumaroyltyramine, also found in eggplant, has demonstrated antihyperglycaemic activity in in vitro studies.

name: Fibre & Scopoletin
description: Eggplant provides 3g dietary fibre per 100g, contributing to gut microbiome diversity and cholesterol regulation. It also contains scopoletin — a coumarin with vasodilatory properties (via smooth muscle relaxation) and antioxidant activity. Direct human RCT data for eggplant specifically are limited; these properties are inferred from its well-established compositional evidence.

name: Apigenin
description: Apigenin is chamomile's principal bioactive flavonoid (~68% of total flavonoid content). It binds to benzodiazepine receptors at the GABA-A receptor complex with moderate affinity, producing anxiolytic and mild sedative effects without dependency risk. The standardised chamomile extract used in the GAD clinical trial (220-1100mg/day, 1.2% apigenin) significantly outperformed placebo on Hamilton Anxiety Scale (p=0.047).

name: Bisabolol & Terpenoids
description: Alpha-bisabolol (levomenol) is the principal sesquiterpene alcohol in chamomile essential oil, contributing anti-inflammatory and skin-healing properties. It inhibits prostaglandin synthesis via cyclooxygenase pathways and has anxiolytic effects in animal models via 5-HT1A receptor modulation (the serotonin receptor targeted by buspirone). Anti-inflammatory activity is consistent with traditional use for gastrointestinal spasm.

name: Matricine & Chamazulene
description: Chamazulene is the characteristic deep-blue compound formed from matricine during steam distillation of chamomile oil. It is a potent inhibitor of leukotriene B4 synthesis (a pro-inflammatory eicosanoid) and has documented antioxidant activity. Combined with apigenin's GABA-A modulation and bisabolol's serotonergic activity, these terpenoids give chamomile a mechanistically plausible multi-target calming profile.
